source_text: Ἐγὼ δὲ εἰ μὲν ἐγένοντό ποτε ἰχθῦς οὐκ ἂν εἴποιμι, ὅτι δὲ ἐν ᾧ ταῦτα ἔγραφον τῶν ἰχθύων ἦσαν ἀλογώτεροι, καὶ πάνυ εὐτόνως διατειναίμην. Ἐξαγαγέτω ἡ γῆ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. Τίνος ἕνεκεν, τοῦ λόγου τρέχοντος ἀθρόως, ἀπεσιώπησα χρόνον οὐκ ὀλίγον, ἴσως θαυμάζουσιν οἱ πολλοί· ἀλλ' οὐχὶ οἵγε φιλοπονώτεροι τῶν ἀκροατῶν ἀγνοοῦσι τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς ἀφασίας. Πῶς γάρ; οἱ διὰ τοῦ πρὸς ἀλλήλους ὁρᾶν καὶ ἐννεύειν ἐπιστρέψαντές με πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς, καὶ εἰς ἔννοιαν ἀγαγόντες τῶν παρεθέντων. Εἶδος γὰρ ὅλον τῆς κτίσεως, καὶ οὐκ ἐλάχιστον τοῦτο, παρέλαθεν ἡμᾶς, καὶ μικροῦ ἀπιὼν ᾤχετο ἀνεξέταστον παντελῶς ὁ λόγος καταλιπών. Ἐξαγαγέτω γὰρ τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν κατὰ γένος, καὶ πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. Εἴπαμεν τὰ περὶ τῶν νηκτῶν, ὅσα ὁ καιρὸς ἐνεδίδου ἑσπέρας· σήμερον μετέβημεν ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν χερσαίων ἐξέτασιν. Διέφυγεν ἡμᾶς τὸ πτηνὸν ἐν τῷ μέσῳ. Ἀνάγκη τοίνυν, κατὰ τοὺς ἐπιλήσμονας τῶν ὁδοιπόρων, οἳ ἐπειδάν τι τῶν καιρίων καταλίπωσι, κἂν ἐπιπολὺ τῆς ὁδοῦ προέλθωσι, πάλιν τὴν αὐτὴν ὑποστρέφουσιν, ἀξίαν τῆς ῥᾳθυμίας δίκην τὸν ἐκ τῆς ὁδοιπορίας κόπον ὑπέχοντες, οὕτω καὶ ἡμῖν, ὡς ἔοικε, τὴν αὐτὴν πάλιν βαδιστέον. Καὶ γὰρ οὐδὲ εὐκαταφρόνητόν ἐστι τὸ παρεθὲν, ἀλλὰ τὸ τρίτον ἔοικεν εἶναι τῆς ἐν τοῖς ζῴοις κτίσεως, εἴπερ τρία ζῴων ἐστὶ γένη, τό τε χερσαῖον, καὶ τὸ πτηνὸν, καὶ τὸ ἔνυδρον. Ἐξαγαγέτω, φησὶ, τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν κατὰ γένος, καὶ πετεινὰ πετόμενα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κατὰ γένος. Διὰ τί ἐξ ὑδάτων καὶ τοῖς πτηνοῖς τὴν γένεσιν ἔδωκεν; Ὅτι ὥσπερ συγγένειά τίς ἐστι τοῖς πετομένοις πρὸς τὰ νηκτά. Καὶ γὰρ ὥσπερ οἱ ἰχθῦς τὸ ὕδωρ τέμνουσι, τῇ μὲν κινήσει τῶν πτερύγων εἰς τὸ πρόσω χωροῦντες, τῇ δὲ τοῦ οὐραίου μεταβολῇ τάς τε περιστροφὰς καὶ τὰς εὐθείας ὁρμὰς ἑαυτοῖς οἰακίζοντες· οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πτηνῶν ἐστιν ἰδεῖν διανηχομένων τὸν ἀέρα τοῖς πτεροῖς κατὰ τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον. Ὥστε ἐπειδὴ ἓν ἰδίωμα ἐν ἑκατέροις τὸ νήχεσθαι, μία τις αὐτοῖς ἡ συγγένεια ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑδάτων γενέσεως παρεσχέθη. Πλήν γε ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν πτηνῶν ἄπουν, διὰ τὸ πᾶσι τὴν δίαιταν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ὑπάρχειν, καὶ πάντα ἀναγκαίως τῆς τῶν ποδῶν ὑπουργίας προσδεῖσθαι. Τοῖς μὲν γὰρ ἁρπακτικοῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν αἱ τῶν ὀνύχων ἀκμαί· τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς, διά τε τὸν πορισμὸν τῆς τροφῆς, καὶ διὰ τὴν λοιπὴν τοῦ βίου διεξαγωγὴν, ἀναγκαία τῶν ποδῶν ἡ ὑπηρεσία δεδώρηται. Ὀλίγοι δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων κακόποδές εἰσιν, οὔτε βαδίζειν οὔτε ἀγρεύειν τοῖς ποσὶν ἐπιτήδειοι· ὡς αἵ τε χελιδόνες εἰσὶ, οὔτε βαδίζειν, οὔτε ἀγρεύειν δυνάμεναι, καὶ αἱ δρεπανίδες λεγό μεναι, οἷς ἡ τροφὴ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ ἀέρι ἐμφερομένων ἐπινενόηται. Χελιδόνι δὲ τὸ τῆς πτήσεως πρόσγειον ἀντὶ τῆς τῶν ποδῶν ὑπηρεσίας ἐστίν. 8.3 Εἰσὶ μέντοι γενῶν διαφοραὶ μυρίαι καὶ ἐν τοῖς ὄρνισιν, ἃς ἐάν τις κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἐπίῃ καθ' ὃν ἐν μέρει καὶ τῆς τῶν ἰχθύων ἐξετάσεως ἐφηψάμεθα, εὑρήσει ἓν μὲν ὄνομα τῶν πετεινῶν, μυρίας δὲ ἐν τούτοις διαφορὰς ἔν τε τοῖς μεγέθεσι καὶ ἐν τοῖς σχήμασι καὶ ἐν ταῖς χρόαις· καὶ κατὰ τοὺς βίους, καὶ τὰς πράξεις, καὶ τὰ ἤθη, ἀμύθητον οὖσαν αὐτοῖς τὴν πρὸς ἄλληλα παραλλαγήν.
thought_title: The omitted birds must be treated
orientation: Basil is preaching on the creation of animals and has just discussed land animals, but he realizes he skipped the birds, which were created on the fifth day from the waters.
pass_a_gloss: But I, if they ever became fish, I would not say; but that in which I was writing these things they were more speechless than the fish, I would very vigorously maintain. Let the earth bring forth a living creature. For what reason, while the discourse was running swiftly, I fell silent for no little time, perhaps the many wonder; but not the more diligent of the hearers are ignorant of the cause of the speechlessness. How so? They who by looking at one another and nodding turned me toward themselves, and brought me to a thought of the things that had been passed over. For a whole kind of the creation, and this not the least, escaped our notice, and the discourse nearly went away leaving it completely unexamined. For let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying upon the earth according to the firmament of heaven. We said the things about the swimming creatures, as much as the occasion allowed in the evening; today we moved on to the examination of the land animals. The winged creature escaped us in the middle. It is necessary therefore, like forgetful travelers, who whenever they leave behind something of the essentials, even if they have gone far along the road, turn back again the same way, paying as a worthy penalty for their carelessness the toil of the journey, so also for us, as it seems, the same road must be walked again. For indeed the thing passed over is not to be despised, but it seems to be the third part of the creation among the animals, if indeed there are three kinds of animals, the land animal, and the winged, and the water-dwelling. Let the waters bring forth, it says, creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying upon the earth according to the firmament of heaven according to kind. Why did he give to the winged creatures also their origin from the waters? Because just as there is a certain kinship of the flying creatures to the swimming creatures. For just as the fish cut the water, moving forward by the motion of their fins, and by the turning of their tail steering for themselves both their turnings and their straight impulses; so also in the case of the winged creatures it is possible to see them swimming through the air with their wings in a similar manner. So that since one peculiar property in both is the swimming, one kinship was provided for them from the origin from the waters. Except that no winged creature is footless, because for all their way of life is from the earth, and all necessarily need the service of feet. For to the predatory ones the sharp points of their claws are for the hunt; to the rest, both for the provision of food and for the rest of the conduct of life, the necessary service of feet has been given. But few of the birds are bad-footed, neither suited for walking nor for hunting with their feet; as the swallows are, neither able to walk nor to hunt, and the ones called scythe-birds, for whom food has been devised from the things carried in the air. For the swallow, the near-ground flight is instead of the service of feet. 8.3 There are indeed countless differences of kinds also among the birds, which if someone examines in the same manner in which we in turn also touched upon the examination of the fish, he will find one name of the winged creatures, but countless differences among them both in sizes and in shapes and in colors; and according to their lives, and their actions, and their habits, the variation among them being beyond telling.

pass_b_english: Now I would not say that I myself was ever a fish, but I would maintain most vigorously that in the passage where I was writing these things, I was more irrational than the fish. “Let the earth bring forth a living creature” (Genesis 1:24). Why, when the discourse was running on so swiftly, did I fall silent for no small time? Perhaps many are wondering, but the more diligent among my hearers know the cause of my speechlessness. How? They are the ones who, by looking at one another and nodding, turned me back to themselves and brought to mind what had been passed over. For a whole class of creation, and not the least important one, had escaped us, and the discourse nearly went on its way leaving it completely unexamined. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying over the earth across the firmament of heaven according to kind” (Genesis 1:20). We spoke about the swimming creatures, as much as the evening allowed; today we moved on to the examination of the land animals. The winged creature slipped through in the middle. So then, like forgetful travelers who, when they leave behind something essential, even if they have gone far along the road, turn back again, paying the penalty for their carelessness with the toil of the journey—so we too, it seems, must walk the same road again. For what was passed over is not something to be despised; it seems to be a third part of the creation of living things, if indeed there are three kinds of living creatures: the land animal, the winged, and the water-dwelling. “Let the waters bring forth,” it says, “creeping things of living souls according to kind, and winged creatures flying over the earth across the firmament of heaven according to kind” (Genesis 1:20). Why did he give the winged creatures their origin from the waters? Because there is a certain kinship between flying creatures and swimming creatures. For just as fish cut through the water, moving forward by the motion of their wings, and steering their turns and straight courses by the movement of their tail, so also in the case of winged creatures one can see them swimming through the air with their wings in a similar way. Therefore, since swimming is one distinctive property in both, a single kinship was provided for them from their origin in the waters. Except that no winged creature is footless, because all of them have their sustenance from the earth, and all necessarily require the service of feet. For the predatory ones have sharp points of claws for the hunt; for the rest, the service of feet has been granted as necessary both for procuring food and for the rest of life's conduct. But a few birds are bad-footed, suited neither for walking nor for hunting with their feet—as the swallows are, unable either to walk or to hunt, and the so-called scythe-birds, whose food is contrived from things carried in the air. For the swallow, its low flight near the ground takes the place of the service of feet. There are, however, countless differences of kinds among the birds, which if someone examines in the same way that we partially took up the examination of the fish, he will find that there is one name for winged creatures, but countless differences among them in sizes and in shapes and in colors; and in their ways of life, their activities, and their habits, their variation from one another is beyond telling.

problems.why: πτερύγων means 'wings,' not 'fins.' Fish don't have wings; this is part of the analogy between fish tails and bird wings.

problems.why: ἀλογώτεροι means 'more irrational/without reason,' not 'more speechless'; speechless is λάλος-related, not λόγος-related.
problems.fix: I was more irrational than the fish
problems.ruling: ἀλογώτεροι means 'more irrational,' not 'more speechless'; the translator already used 'speechless' for ἀφασίας, conflating two words.

problems.source_quote: ἐν μέρει καὶ τῆς τῶν ἰχθύων ἐξετάσεως ἐφηψάμεθα
problems.why: ἐν μέρει means 'in part' or 'partially,' not 'in turn.' Basil says they examined fish only partially, not that they took turns.
problems.fix: as we partially took up the examination of the fish
problems.ruling: ἐν μέρει means 'in part,' not 'in turn'; Basil says the fish examination was partial, a meaning change.

fixed.note: ἀλογώτεροι means 'more irrational', and the verb ἦσαν is plural: Basil means the writers who claimed humans came from fish, not himself, so the sentence also needs its subject changed, e.g. 'Whether they were ever fish I would not say, but I would maintain most vigorously that when they wrote these things they were more irrational than the fish.'
